transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-29 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maria Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Laura Stein (Veridian Head of AI), Ravi Mehta (Platform Eng), Sophie Alvarez (CTO)

Summary: Quick hosted API product walkthrough focused on chat and text generation basics. Live demo included streaming responses, adjusting parameters, and notes on retry strategies and console observability.

[00:00] Maria Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Maria from Redwood Inference, and with me is Daniel Park, our solutions engineer. happy to run through the hosted API demo and cover streaming and retries.
[00:18] Laura Stein: Thanks Maria. we are excited — main goal for today is to understand latency profiles and how streaming works, and what controls we have for cost.
[00:29] Maria Chen: great. quick agenda — 1) product overview, 2) live demo of chat / text generation, 3) streaming and params, 4) retries/backoff and best practices, 5) console observability and optimize suggestions, then q&a and next steps. sound good?
[00:44] Sophie Alvarez: Yep, that works. we have Rahul... sorry Ravi and Laura — we are mainly evaluating hosted vs dedicated.
[00:53] Daniel Park: cool, i'll kick off the demo. quick note: our hosted API exposes endpoints for chat and text generation, embeddings, and we support streaming via SSE and chunked responses. some of the transcript sh- the auto transcriber sometimes writes SSE as 's s e' so just heads up.
[01:10] Daniel Park: (screen share) here's the basic POST to /v1/chat/completions — you send messages, model, and typical params: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty, and an optional stop sequence. we also have a simpler text-generation endpoint which is similar.
[01:30] Ravi Mehta: how do you recommend we set temperature/top_p for user-facing summarization vs creative content?
[01:38] Daniel Park: good q. for deterministic summarization we keep temperature at 0 to 0.2, top_p near 1.0 but you can reduce if you want narrower output. for creative outputs you bump temperature 0.7-1.0. also max_tokens controls both cost and truncation risk. our console shows per-request token estimates so you can tune.
[01:58] Maria Chen: quick thing on cost — we show token-level cost breakdown in the Console. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles and batching rules to reduce per-token costs for steady workloads.
[02:12] Laura Stein: Are there built-in batchings? we have a lot of small requests from the storefront.
[02:18] Daniel Park: yes, automatic batching in the runtime—workload-aware batching. in hosted you can configure batching windows via the Console, and Optimize will suggest batch sizes based on latency SLOs.
[02:32] Daniel Park: ok streaming demo — i'm going to send a chat request with stream=true. you should see partial chunks as the model generates. note that streaming is server-sent events, so on the client we parse each event and render progressively.
[02:50] [03:00] (streaming demo)
[03:05] Daniel Park: you'll see the SSE frames arriving — sometimes the transcriber writes them as brackets — but the important bit is the 'delta' chunks which contain incremental tokens. this reduces time-to-first-token and creates a snappier UX.
[03:25] Laura Stein: that's helpful. what's typical TTFB for streaming?
[03:29] Daniel Park: depends on model size and prompt. for our curated smaller chat models you can see ~150-300ms TTFB on average in hosted EU/US regions; big models 400ms+. we expose percentiles in Console so you can verify.
[03:45] Sophie Alvarez: do you support webhooks for completions or only polling/streaming?
[03:50] Maria Chen: hosted supports streaming and standard request/response. webhooks for async jobs is part of our roadmap for large-batch offline jobs; for real-time we recommend streaming or short-polling.
[04:05] Ravi Mehta: what about retries — how do we handle 429s and transient 5xx?
[04:10] Daniel Park: best practice is exponential backoff with jitter. include an idempotency key on requests that can be retried safely — for completions it's usually safe to retry for network errors but not always for user-visible side effects. we also provide guidance to honor 429 Retry-After headers and we recommend client-side rate limiting to avoid thundering herds.
[04:35] Laura Stein: can we get a sample client snippet for streaming + retry logic?
[04:38] Daniel Park: yes i'll share a Gist and the benchmark spreadsheet after this call — i'll include SSE parsing and an example backoff implementation.
[04:48] Maria Chen: security and compliance quick note — hosted API supports SOC 2 controls, SSO (SAML/OIDC), and customer-managed KMS keys for encryption at rest in our private deployments; for hosted we integrate with standard KMS offerings and provide audit logs in the Console.
[05:07] Sophie Alvarez: how about data retention, do you retain prompts/outputs?
[05:12] Maria Chen: by default we retain logs for 30 days for debugging but you can opt out, and enterprise contracts allow retention policies or no retention. we'll share our security whitepaper.
[05:23] Ravi Mehta: ok good. back to params: what about stop sequences? any gotchas?
[05:28] Daniel Park: stop sequences are simple but watch for them being substrings of expected content — it's safer to design explicit stop tokens when possible. for chat flows we also support structured output via function/tool calling which is more reliable than ad-hoc stop tokens for extraction tasks.
[05:45] Laura Stein: function calling — is that available on hosted?
[05:48] Daniel Park: yes, we support function calls — you can pass callable schemas and the model will return structured JSON. small note: sometimes the transcriber writes JSON as 'jay son' — ha.
[06:02] Maria Chen: demoing Console now — here's the per-route metrics, latency percentiles, token cost breakdowns, and a trace view that ties a request to the underlying infra. you can filter by model, region, and time window.
[06:20] [06:35] (Console screenshot walkthrough)
[06:40] Daniel Park: Optimize module highlights recommendations like quantization for a given model, batch window recommendations, and cacheable prefix suggestions. it will also surface quality regressions if you hook up evals.
[06:56] Laura Stein: could Optimize recommend switching to a cheaper model variant when load is high?
[07:00] Daniel Park: yes, Optimize plus smart routing can suggest fallback policies — e.g., route to a distilled model for non-critical requests, keep a faster model for low-latency endpoints.
[07:12] Ravi Mehta: do you provide SDKs, or are we doing raw HTTP?
[07:16] Maria Chen: we have official SDKs in Python, Node, and Go — they handle streaming parsing and retries and are open-source.
[07:25] Sophie Alvarez: any pitfalls we should watch for when using streaming with heavy concurrency?
[07:30] Daniel Park: common pitfall is not bounding concurrent SSE connections — you need a connection pool and reuse logic on the client. also watch memory with long-running streams and implement backpressure.
[07:45] Laura Stein: latency SLOs — what SLAs do you offer on hosted?
[07:50] Maria Chen: hosted has a standard SLA for uptime; latency SLOs are in Dedicated where we can guarantee percentiles. for hosted we publish observed percentiles and can discuss enterprise add-ons for tighter SLOs.
[08:04] Ravi Mehta: network security — do you offer VPC peering or private link?
[08:09] Maria Chen: for hosted we support PrivateLink/Cloud Interconnect options for enterprise plans, and Redwood Private is for full VPC/on-prem deployments. we'll include the network options in the security pack.
[08:25] Daniel Park: back to retries — we also recommend using short idempotency tokens for the parts of your flow that can be retried; for example when you persist the model output server-side, persist first then acknowledge to the user.
[08:40] Laura Stein: do you support partial retries when streaming fails mid-response?
[08:45] Daniel Park: streaming partials are trickier. the recommended approach is to treat the stream as append-only and on fatal errors restart the request with the same prompt and an idempotency key; you'll likely get a slightly different completion so for exact continuity you might need server-side reconciliation.
[09:05] Sophie Alvarez: any recommendation on model choice for product search summarization?
[09:10] Daniel Park: for product summarization we often recommend a compact chat model tuned for instruction-following — it gives lower cost and faster latency. Optimize can suggest a model/quantization pairing after we see your sample payloads.
[09:28] Laura Stein: sample payloads — we have a few typical user queries and 95th percentile prompt lengths around 1.2k tokens.
[09:36] Daniel Park: cool — that's helpful. long prompts increase KV cache pressure on the runtime so we'll look at that in the benchmark.
[09:45] Maria Chen: i see a question in the chat about retries on streamed chunks vs full request retries — daniel partially covered this but we'll include a doc link.
[09:56] Daniel Park: also recommend enabling prefix caching for common system prompts to save cost and reduce latency when you have repeat prefixes.
[10:08] Laura Stein: does prefix caching affect model consistency or can it cause stale behavior?
[10:13] Daniel Park: prefix caching is safe if the prefix is static; for dynamic system context avoid caching. we also version model prompts to ensure consistency.
[10:26] [10:40] (Demo: showing quick sample requests and streaming)
[11:00] Laura Stein: what's the typical retry budget you see?
[11:05] Daniel Park: depends on load and error patterns — generally keep retry attempts low (2-3) with exponential backoff and jitter; monitor 429/5xx rates in Console and scale or throttle accordingly.
[11:20] Ravi Mehta: for pricing — do you charge per token only or any per-request surcharge for streaming?
[11:25] Maria Chen: pricing is per-token for generation and embeddings, no extra per-request streaming surcharge. there are enterprise options for reserved capacity with committed monthly usage which changes unit economics.
[11:40] Sophie Alvarez: how do you recommend instrumenting cost alerts?
[11:44] Daniel Park: use Console per-route cost dashboards and create alerts on token spend or cost per model; we also export billing metrics to your metrics stack if you want to integrate.
[11:58] Laura Stein: if we do a pilot, what's a reasonable scope?
[12:03] Maria Chen: typical pilot is 2-4 weeks: share sample payloads, we run benchmarks, tune batching and caching, and produce a cost/latency report plus Optimize recommendations.
[12:12] Ravi Mehta: ok that sounds good.
[12:15] [12:30] (discussion about pilot logistics)
[12:40] Maria Chen: recap and next steps — i'll send pricing and security docs, daniel will send benchmark template and SSE snippet, ravi will share sample payloads and peak QPS, and let's schedule pilot kickoff the week of 2026-05-04.
[12:58] Laura Stein: thanks everyone. one last thing — any known incompatibilities with our infra (we run kubernetes on GCP)?
[13:05] Daniel Park: none for hosted — for Private we do a kube-based deployment and provide helm charts; we'll cover that in the security pack.
[13:15] Sophie Alvarez: ok great.
[13:20] Maria Chen: thanks all — we'll follow up in email with the docs.

End of meeting.
